title: NVIDIA Blackwell (B200 / GB200)
hook: Blackwell is the chip the 2025 frontier ran on: a two-die GPU with an FP4 transformer engine, built to train and serve trillion-parameter models.
key_points: NVIDIA's GPU architecture announced at GTC 2024, successor to Hopper (H100).
The B200 packs two dies into one GPU; GB200 pairs Blackwell GPUs with a Grace CPU.
A second-gen Transformer Engine adds 4-bit (FP4) precision for faster inference.
NVIDIA claims large training and inference speedups over H100 at better energy efficiency.
content_html: Blackwell is NVIDIA's GPU architecture unveiled at GTC in March 2024, the successor to the Hopper generation that trained most of the early LLM boom. Its data-center parts — the B200 GPU and the GB200 superchip — were built specifically for the scale of frontier AI, and they became the hardware backbone for training and serving the largest 2025-era models.
extra_html:
How it works

The B200 is physically two GPU dies fused into one package connected by a high-bandwidth link, so it behaves as a single very large GPU. The GB200 superchip pairs Blackwell GPUs with NVIDIA's Grace CPU over a fast interconnect for rack-scale systems. The headline feature for AI is a second-generation Transformer Engine that supports 4-bit floating point (FP4), letting inference run at far higher throughput by trading a controlled amount of precision — the hardware counterpart to quantization techniques.

Why it matters

Frontier model capability is gated as much by available compute as by ideas, so each GPU generation resets what is trainable. NVIDIA marketed Blackwell with large multipliers over H100 for both training and inference; whatever the exact numbers, the practical effect was that trillion-parameter training and cheap large-model inference became routine. It is a concrete instance of the hardware lottery: the models that won were the ones these chips ran best.

related.title: Why GPUs Power Deep Learning
related.hook: Neural networks are parallel by nature, and a GPU runs thousands of threads at once - so the same math that crawls on a CPU maps naturally onto a GPU and trains far faster.

related.title: In-Datacenter Performance Analysis of a TPU
related.hook: Google built a custom chip whose heart is a 256x256 grid of 8-bit multiply-accumulate units - and in production it ran neural-net inference roughly 15-30x faster than the GPUs and CPUs of its day.

related.title: Mixed Precision Training
related.hook: Store weights, activations, and gradients in 16-bit floats to roughly halve memory - but keep a 32-bit master copy of the weights and scale the loss so tiny gradients don't vanish.
